source: Hartung et al. (2023) Deep Anomaly Detection on Tennessee Eastman Process Data
finding: A benchmark of 27 deep unsupervised anomaly detectors on Tennessee Eastman (TEP) found almost every method scores very high. The ranking among them is therefore weakly informative.
numbers: Best F1 values around 0.97 (TCN-S2S-AE 0.9699, Dense-AE 0.9632, LSTM-AE 0.9631); best AUPRC about 0.99; even the lowest listed F1 is about 0.907. Best-F1 and AUPRC used; each method tuned with a 24 h budget.
quote: All methods have yielded high scores.
limits: Synthetic simulated data with faults injected into fault-free runs; threshold chosen at best F1 on labels, which inflates scores.
agent_relevance: Saturated benchmark numbers cannot be used to choose a detector. Our agent should not trust 'state of the art on TEP' claims.

source: Hartung et al. (2023) Deep Anomaly Detection on Tennessee Eastman Process Data
finding: An untrained LSTM autoencoder (random weights) was included as a baseline and ranked in the upper half of trained methods.
numbers: Untrained-LSTM-AE: F1 0.9335 (rank 9), AUPRC 0.9792 (rank 14), mean rank 10 of 27; trained OmniAnomaly F1 0.9334, USAD 0.9333.
limits: Baseline proposed by Kim et al. 2022; shows the benchmark is easy, not that random nets are good detectors in plants.
agent_relevance: A trivial baseline that nearly ties trained models is a warning sign. Our scaffold should always run a null baseline before crediting a clever detector.

source: Hartung et al. (2023) Deep Anomaly Detection on Tennessee Eastman Process Data
finding: The authors state their own caveat: scores are high because the data are synthetic with defined faults; real plant data will be harder and labelling the anomalies is the challenge.
numbers: 27 methods evaluated on one modified TEP dataset; time-series F1 and AUPRC.
quote: The task will be considerably more challenging for actual chemical process data.
limits: F1 and AUPRC cannot assess longer periods and interdependent points in time series.
agent_relevance: Benchmark success is conditional on easy fault persistence and clean labels.

source: Hartung, Muraleedharan, Kloft, Burger (2026) Beyond Tennessee Eastman: Benchmarking Deep Anomaly Detection on Real-World Pilot-Scale Continuous Distillation Data
finding: The same group repeated its benchmark on real pilot-plant distillation data (n-butanol/water, OME purification, a water case) and found a large drop from TEP.
numbers: 30 methods (26 deep, 4 classical) via TimeSeAD. Mean F1 0.859 and AUPRC 0.906 on TEP versus mean F1 0.532 and AUPRC 0.361 on the three pilot datasets. No method exceeded F1 0.718 or AUPRC 0.597.
quote: TEP achieves high average scores; performance on the pilot-plant datasets is substantially lower across all cases.
limits: Pilot-scale plants, three datasets, known anomaly onset times so label noise is ruled out; results depend on metric and dataset.
agent_relevance: Strongest evidence that TEP results do not transfer. Treat any TEP-based accuracy claim as an upper bound.

source: Hartung, Muraleedharan, Kloft, Burger (2026) Beyond Tennessee Eastman: Benchmarking Deep Anomaly Detection on Real-World Pilot-Scale Continuous Distillation Data
finding: On the real data, deep methods still beat classical baselines, but no deep family wins consistently and ranking changes with metric.
numbers: Best deep vs best shallow F1: butanol 0.624 vs 0.588; OME 0.718 vs 0.666; water 0.531 vs 0.433; mean 0.624 vs 0.562. Best method differs by dataset (LSTM-2S2-P on Butanol and Water; LSTM-VAE and LSTM-DVAE on OME). Dataset mean F1: butanol 0.538, OME 0.629, water 0.428.
limits: Margin over shallow baselines is 0.05 to 0.10 F1; hybrid methods best on average but weak on some datasets. Dataset-to-column mapping in the extracted table is partly garbled.
agent_relevance: Method choice is dataset-specific; advise testing several detectors and reporting the spread, not one winner.

source: Hartung, Muraleedharan, Kloft, Burger (2026) Beyond Tennessee Eastman: Benchmarking Deep Anomaly Detection on Real-World Pilot-Scale Continuous Distillation Data
finding: The paper lists benchmark inflation sources: hyperparameters tuned on a small set of standard faults, persistent fault states, and no advanced control layers (MPC/APC) in TEP.
numbers: Cites that an untrained LSTM autoencoder reaches F1 above 0.93 on TEP; reports anomalies in plants often appear first in control actions rather than outputs; fault dynamics of 10 to 60 minutes force a trade-off between detection reliability and alarm latency.
limits: Argument paper plus benchmark; some claims are cited from other work.
agent_relevance: Detection should use manipulated variables and control behaviour, not only measurements. Our agent should ask which signals the controller hides.

source: Gao, Wang, Chen (2024) Autoencoder-assisted Feature Ensemble Net for Incipient Faults
finding: Faults 3, 9 and 15 of TEP (small step, random-variation and sticking faults, the hardest) are undetectable by most statistical and unsupervised deep methods; the authors say deep nets also fail even with prior information.
numbers: Table I fault detection rate (FDR) on faults 3 / 9 / 15: PCA 5.70 / 7.70 / 3.05 %; DPCA 10.40 / 12.85 / 2.25 %; MD 2.65 / 5.55 / 1.30 %; KPCA 2.60 / 3.75 / 0.95 %; sparse PCA 1.05 / 1.65 / 0.80 %. The same PCA gets 99.95% on faults 1 and 4.
quote: Faults 3, 9 and 15 ... lacking effective detection technologies in the field of fault detection.
limits: Detection rates are the authors' own reproduction on 960-sample test runs; further table columns garbled in extraction so only five named methods are quoted.
agent_relevance: Three of 21 faults are almost signal-free in standard sensors; any agent claiming full TEP coverage should be doubted.

source: Gao, Wang, Chen (2024) Autoencoder-assisted Feature Ensemble Net for Incipient Faults
finding: A feature-ensemble approach (AE-FENet) is claimed to reach over 96% average detection on faults 3, 9 and 15.
numbers: Average FDR 98.66% with max lag lmax = 2; faults 3, 9, 15 reach 97.55%, 97.55%, 96.05%; plain FENet (PCA features) averages 85.73% with faults 5, 15, 16, 21 each under 90%. Earlier temporal deep nets cited at 96%, 92%, 70% on faults 3, 9, 15.
limits: Single group; thresholds and windows tuned on TEP; no independent replication found this session. Compare SensorSCAN where faults 9 and 15 stay undetected unsupervised.
agent_relevance: Claims on 3, 9, 15 conflict across papers (see b11); treat as unreplicated and check false alarm rate before trusting.

source: Xiao, Kordon, Sen (2023) Fault Detection and Diagnosis in Tennessee Eastman Process with Deep Autoencoder
finding: A deep autoencoder (DAE) beat PCA-based T2 and SPE on most TEP faults in detection rate and false alarm rate, and gives variable contributions for root-cause hints.
numbers: DAE FDR 90% or higher with at most 3% FAR on faults 1, 2, 6, 8, 12, 13, 14, 17, 18; faults 3, 9, 15: DAE FDR 3.6, 3.5, 7.9 (none satisfactory); fault 21 DAE 43%; faults 10, 11, 16, 19, 20, 21 poor for all methods. PCA used 9 PCs.
limits: Single split, 21 faults; DAE FAR up to 7.5% (fault 16). Some table columns garbled.
agent_relevance: DAE gains are on faults linear methods already half-detect; hardest faults unchanged.

source: Xiao, Kordon, Sen (2023) Fault Detection and Diagnosis in Tennessee Eastman Process with Deep Autoencoder
finding: Detection delay shows the autoencoder is not uniformly faster than classical statistics.
numbers: Delay (minutes) DAE vs T2 vs SPE: fault 3: 159 vs 42 vs 60; fault 13: 27 vs 138 vs 108; fault 20: 216 vs 21 vs 33; fault 21: 819 vs 63 vs 36; fault 1: 0 vs 21 vs 6.
limits: Delay only on detected faults at fixed thresholds; mixed result.
agent_relevance: Report detection delay alongside rate. Scoring a detector by hit rate alone overrates slow detectors.

source: Golyadkin et al. (2023) SensorSCAN: Self-supervised learning and deep clustering for fault diagnosis in chemical processes
finding: Unsupervised deep clustering with self-supervised pretraining (SensorSCAN) detects far more TEP faults than PCA and a convolutional autoencoder, on two public TEP variants.
numbers: Faults detected: SensorSCAN 90% (TEPRieth, 20 faults) and 87% (TEPRicker, 28 faults), 96% of those correctly diagnosed; PCA left 12 of 20 and 17 of 28 faults undetected; ConvAE left 8 of 20 and 11 of 28. Average delay 27.7 and 28.47 time stamps versus 49.95 and 52.28 for ConvAE. Claim +0.2 to 0.3 TPR at fixed FPR.
limits: Unsupervised label matching is imperfect; faults 9 and 15 (and 16 and 21 on Ricker) stay undetected by all unsupervised models.
agent_relevance: Even strong unsupervised models cannot see faults 9 and 15 without labels, in contrast to the Gao et al. claim (b08).

source: Golyadkin et al. (2023) SensorSCAN: Self-supervised learning and deep clustering for fault diagnosis in chemical processes
finding: Fine-tuning on a single labelled run nearly matches a supervised GRU trained on all labelled data, so labels help a lot but few are needed.
numbers: Highest TPR in 14 faults for SensorSCAN single-run versus 15 for the all-runs GRU on TEPRieth (17 versus 26 on TEPRicker); only the all-runs GRU detected fault 9 on TEPRieth; fault 15 stayed hard for all models.
limits: Simulated data; single-run labels from a simulator are cleaner than plant labels.
agent_relevance: A few labelled examples per fault go a long way; in-context examples of past faults may be the analogue for our agent.

source: Golyadkin et al. (2023) SensorSCAN: Self-supervised learning and deep clustering for fault diagnosis in chemical processes
finding: Clustering quality for unsupervised fault grouping is low for classical and older deep baselines on TEP, so diagnosis is harder than detection.
numbers: Clustering ACC / ARI / NMI on TEPRieth: ConvAE 0.175 / 0.113 / 0.222; another baseline 0.274 / 0.110 / 0.363; the proposed method 0.402 / 0.124 / 0.467 in the first reading of the table (layout partly garbled).
limits: Row labels are ambiguous in the extracted table; use only as order of magnitude.
agent_relevance: Separating fault types without labels remains hard.

source: Pal et al. (2025/26) A Compact CNN-Transformer Model for Robust Fault Diagnosis in Large-Scale Chemical Processes
finding: On TEP supervised 19-class diagnosis, accuracy is near saturation; a CNN-Transformer gains only 0.06 points over a tuned LSTM.
numbers: Accuracy 99.92% vs 99.86% (absolute +0.06%); macro F1 higher for the CNN-Transformer; variation across seeds below 0.03%; 80/10/10 split by simulation run, 500 samples per run at 3-minute sampling, fault onset after index 160.
limits: Run-level split is good practice; single dataset where prior work already reports near 100%.
agent_relevance: Saturation means the benchmark cannot discriminate models.

source: Pal et al. (2025/26) A Compact CNN-Transformer Model for Robust Fault Diagnosis in Large-Scale Chemical Processes
finding: The authors cite near-saturation accuracy on TEP for recent recurrent and transformer models, matching their own 99.86% LSTM.
numbers: Cites Agarwal et al. 2022 and Verma et al. 2022 as reporting near-saturation results; this paper's models reach 99.86% and 99.92%.
limits: Cited works not opened by this agent.
agent_relevance: Strengthens b01 and b14: supervised TEP accuracy is a solved metric.

source: Pozdnyakov et al. (2024) Adversarial Attacks and Defenses in Fault Detection and Diagnosis: A Comprehensive Benchmark on the Tennessee Eastman Process
finding: Neural fault classifiers on TEP are highly vulnerable to adversarial input perturbations; defences cost accuracy on clean data.
numbers: Clean accuracy: MLP 0.8873, GRU 0.9067, TCN 0.8985. TCN after adversarial training: 0.90 (none) to about 0.77-0.78 (FGSM/PGD, eps 0.1); autoencoder defence 0.75-0.77. Six attack types and five defences tested; a new defence (adversarial training plus data quantisation) proposed.
quote: strong vulnerability of models to adversarial samples
limits: Window 32; three architectures only; attacks assume attacker access to the sensor data path.
agent_relevance: Accuracy under attack, not only clean accuracy, belongs in a diagnosis check; our agent should treat sensor-data integrity as a hypothesis.

source: Khan et al. (2024) FaultExplainer: Leveraging Large Language Models for Interpretable Fault Detection and Diagnosis
finding: FaultExplainer wraps PCA T2 detection and top-contributing-variable ranking in an LLM (GPT-4o, o1-preview) that names root causes on TEP.
numbers: With a given list of 15 candidate root causes: among the 11 faults PCA can detect, GPT-4o classifies 7 and o1-preview 9 correctly. Neither names faults 5 and 10. Without the list: both give a correct or related cause for 8 of the 11 detected faults; neither gets faults 10 and 13.
quote: neither model is able to identify the correct root causes for Faults 10 and 13
limits: Only 11 detectable faults; correctness judged by authors with alias rules; no repeats or variance; descriptive evaluation.
agent_relevance: LLM diagnosis is capped by the statistical detector (PCA misses 4 of 15 faults) and fails on indirect or compensated faults.

source: Khan et al. (2024) FaultExplainer: Leveraging Large Language Models for Interpretable Fault Detection and Diagnosis
finding: The stronger reasoning model (o1-preview) beat GPT-4o when a root-cause list was provided; both failed on the same faults.
numbers: 9/11 vs 7/11 correct with list; shared failures on fault 5 (condenser cooling water inlet, step) and fault 10 (C feed temperature, random variation).
limits: Two-fault difference out of 11; no significance test.
agent_relevance: Controller-masked faults are the failure class, consistent with Hartung 2026 on control actions (b06). Hypothesis tests should look at manipulated variables.

source: Liang and Sin (2026) A Large Language Model Enhanced Fault Diagnosis Framework for Chemical Processes
finding: An MCP-based LLM agent calls a CNN diagnosis tool and an ensemble tool and writes an operator report; ten or so LLMs compared on TEP using LLM-as-judge for accuracy, tool adherence and report quality.
numbers: Ensemble multi-scale CNN accuracy 73.67% vs 68.04% for single model on difficult faults. Tool rule: use single model if max probability >= 0.95, else call ensemble. Upper bound of LLM fault accuracy about 0.83 even at 100% tool adherence.
quote: reliable tool calling and uncertainty-aware reasoning are more critical than model size
limits: Scores from an LLM judge; per-model values lost in PDF extraction so not quoted.
agent_relevance: The agent is bounded by the tool it calls; reliable tool calling and uncertainty reporting matter more than model size.

source: Liang and Sin (2026) A Large Language Model Enhanced Fault Diagnosis Framework for Chemical Processes
finding: Model size did not predict performance; commercial models were consistent and open models weaker.
numbers: Gemini-2.5-Flash-Lite worse than Gemini-2.5-Flash; gpt-4o-mini about equal to gpt-4o; deepseek-chat-v3.1 best of the open models; llama-3.1-8b, qwen3-235b and llama-3.3-70b clearly poorer despite very different sizes.
limits: Qualitative ordering only; numeric table not recoverable.
agent_relevance: Test the scaffold on several model sizes; do not assume bigger is better for tool-using diagnosis.

source: Liang and Sin (2026) A Large Language Model Enhanced Fault Diagnosis Framework for Chemical Processes
finding: A low-confidence case shows the intended behaviour: the LLM reports a low top-class probability and alternatives rather than a confident guess.
numbers: Sample 4201: top class fault 15 at about 30%; alternatives fault 21 (29.17%) and fault 9 (11.84%); judge gave fault accuracy 0.5, tool adherence 1, report quality 5.
limits: One illustrative example.
agent_relevance: Matches the schema guardrail to report uncertainty; confusable classes 9, 15, 21 are exactly the hard ones.

source: Zhou and Zhu (2023) On the optimality of Kalman Filter for Fault Detection
finding: Kalman-filter residual generation is not optimal for fault detection despite its statistical elegance; an optimal filter scheme (OEFB) does better, including on TEP faults 3, 9, 15.
numbers: On 21 TEP faults, KF mean FDR rises as a tuning parameter s goes from 0 to 80 but false alarms rise too; KF matches OEFB's FDR only for s > 20 and then has worse FAR; KF detection delay is poor at every s tested. Table 4 (FDR on faults 3, 9, 15) favours OEFB (values garbled in extraction).
limits: Theory plus Monte Carlo plus one dataset; improvement is relative to one performance index.
agent_relevance: Classical model-based detection has headroom; the chosen index (FDR, FAR, delay) decides which method is called optimal.

source: Downs and Vogel (1993) A plant-wide industrial process control problem
finding: Defined the Tennessee Eastman challenge process and its disturbances, which became the de facto benchmark for process fault detection.
numbers: Not opened. Cited in Hartung 2023, Golyadkin 2023 and Pal as the origin of the benchmark; 21 standard faults.
limits: Not read this session.
agent_relevance: Benchmark origin; read before using TEP claims.

source: Rieth, Amsel, Tran, Cook (2017) Additional Tennessee Eastman Process Simulation Data for Anomaly Detection Evaluation
finding: Public extended TEP dataset with 500 simulation runs per state, used as TEPRieth in several papers.
numbers: Not opened. Per Golyadkin 2023: 500 train and 500 test runs per state, 21,000 runs total, 3-minute sampling, 500 and 960 time stamps per run.
limits: Numbers from a secondary description.
agent_relevance: Fixes run-level splits and seeds; adopt for reproducible tests.

source: Kim et al. (2022) Towards a Rigorous Evaluation of Time-Series Anomaly Detection
finding: Source of the untrained LSTM-AE baseline; shows lenient evaluation inflates anomaly detector scores.
numbers: Not opened. Cited in Hartung 2023 and 2026 (untrained baseline F1 above 0.93 on TEP).
limits: Not read this session.
agent_relevance: Metric choice can create apparent progress; guardrail for our scoring.

source: Isermann (2005) Model-based fault-detection and diagnosis: status and applications
finding: Classic review of fault detection: limit checking, signal models, process models (residual, parity, observer) and classification.
numbers: Not opened. No numbers; the three-way split (expert, model-based, data-driven) is repeated in the opened Pozdnyakov 2024 paper.
limits: Not read this session.
agent_relevance: Taxonomy for the schema's detection versus diagnosis split.
